opus-5.5.text:
I think it's both, and that's normal at this stage of the industry.

On the cooperation side, a lot of agent companies are building on top of foundation models, including ours. We want that ecosystem to be large. If many teams use our model to build products for specific scenarios, that helps us understand what the model can and can't do, and it pushes us to improve long-context, tool use, and reasoning. So in that sense, they're partners, and we should make the model and API as useful to them as possible.

On the competition side, the boundary between "model" and "agent" is getting blurry. As models get stronger, more of what used to be product engineering, like workflow orchestration, planning, and memory, gets absorbed into the model. So some things an agent company builds today might become native model capabilities tomorrow. That creates natural overlap, and we may end up serving the same users.

I don't think we should be too anxious about that, though. The most important thing for us is still to push the intelligence ceiling. If the model is good enough, there will be enough room for many companies. Application companies that really understand a vertical, its users, data, and workflows, will keep their value, because that knowledge doesn't come for free from a better model.

So my view is: cooperate where the value is complementary, compete where it overlaps, and let users decide. In the long run, what matters is who creates real value, not how the categories are drawn today.

r001.rationale: The response describes model capabilities absorbing agent features and creating overlap, but does not link a steep R&D curve to agent companies needing to adjust product strategies dynamically.

r002.rationale: It says vertical knowledge and workflows retain value, but does not raise whether agent companies can build tools or environments that others cannot replicate.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that first-party products have an integration advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's both, and it will stay both for a while. Let me try to explain how I see the layers.

At the base there's the model. Our bet at Moonshot has always been that the model is the product. Agent capability isn't something you bolt on afterwards with prompts and workflow glue. It comes from long context, from reasoning, from the model being able to plan across many steps and recover when a tool call fails. So the deepest value sits in the model, and that's what we focus on.

Then above that you have companies like MindOS building agent frameworks, memory systems, personalized assistants, vertical products. For them we are a supplier. They call our API, they fine-tune on our open weights, and if our model gets better their product gets better overnight without them changing a line of code. That's cooperation in the most natural sense. We want as many of them as possible to succeed, because every agent built on top of us is distribution we didn't have to pay for.

Where it becomes competition is at the boundary. Every time the model takes a step forward, some layer of scaffolding that used to be a company's moat gets absorbed. Two years ago you needed a retrieval system to handle a long document. Now you paste it in. A year ago you needed orchestration logic to decompose a task. Now the model does that itself. So if an agent company's entire differentiation lives in that thin layer, they will feel us coming. I don't think that's hostile. It's just gravity.

So my advice to teams like MindOS, and frankly to ourselves with Kimi, is to build where the model will not go. Deep user relationships, proprietary data, domain workflows, trust in a specific vertical. Those don't get absorbed by the next training run. The orchestration layer does.

I'd also say the industry benefits from this tension. If the agent companies push us hard with real use cases, we get better signal on what capabilities matter. And if we move fast, they're forced to find the places where they're genuinely irreplaceable. I'd rather have that than a comfortable division of labor that nobody tests.

So cooperation on the stack, competition at the boundary, and I expect the boundary to keep moving upward. Which side of it you want to be on is a strategic choice, and I'm not sure anyone gets to choose both forever.

r001.rationale: The response says model advances absorb agent companies’ scaffolding and that teams are forced to find places where they are irreplaceable, linking technological progress to strategic adjustment.

r002.rationale: It advises building around user relationships, data, workflows, and trust that the model will not absorb, but does not raise whether agent companies can build tools or environments that others cannot replicate.

r003.rationale: The response describes agent companies using Moonshot’s API and benefiting from model improvements, but does not state that first-party products have an integration advantage.

astra-6.text:
I think cooperation and competition will coexist. We focus on improving the underlying models, while agent companies focus on turning those capabilities into products that solve particular problems. There’s a lot of room to work together, because a stronger model can help them build better agents, and their applications can help us understand what capabilities are still missing.

Of course, as models and products evolve, there may be areas where we overlap. I don’t think that means the relationship has to become purely competitive. The key is whether each company creates distinct value for users. The boundary will keep moving, so I’d approach it as an open relationship rather than draw a permanent line between partners and competitors.

sol-6.1.text:
I think cooperation and competition will coexist. From our perspective, the foundation model is a platform, and agent companies can build applications on top of it. They understand particular user needs and workflows, while we focus on improving the model’s underlying capabilities. There’s a lot of room to work together there.

Of course, as models become more capable and we explore products ourselves, some overlap is inevitable. The important question is whether we’re creating value for users. I don’t think the model company has to do every application, or that an agent company’s value disappears as models improve. The boundary will keep evolving, and so will the relationship.
